title: Who Makes It Through the Change?

scenes.tts: A red blight moves into a forest where the trees look alike. What decides whether this population continues or disappears? Watch the trees, their blue resistance bars, and the yellow seeds that mark a next generation.
scenes.caption: A red blight moves into a forest where the trees look alike. What decides whether this population continues or disappears? Watch the trees, their blue resistance bars, and the yellow seeds that mark a next generation.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP FOR BOTH FILMS: living chestnut trunks, leaves, and roots GREEN; inherited resistance bars BLUE; blight and cankers RED; seeds and offspring YELLOW; dead or nonreproducing tissue GREY. Build one carried 16:9 forest with eight large cartoon chestnuts filling 70% of the frame. Red specks drift in from the left while branches sway. On the question, a white question mark grows above the forest. Blue bars rise inside the trunks and yellow seed icons glow near the ground. No title yet.
scenes.narration: A red blight moves into a forest where the trees look alike. What decides whether this population continues or disappears? Watch the trees, their blue resistance bars, and the yellow seeds that mark a next generation.

scenes.visual: Keep branches swaying and red specks drifting. Fade in the title 'Who Makes It Through the Change?' in large white text above the carried forest, then fade it out. The resistance bars continue a slow pulse.

scenes.tts: After a change, some members of a population die and some live. Living members may reproduce. Some migrate, meaning they move elsewhere, where they must still survive. A species is extinct only when no living members remain anywhere. Losing a species from one forest is not the same thing.
scenes.caption: After a change, some members of a population die and some live. Living members may reproduce. Some migrate, meaning they move elsewhere, where they must still survive. A species is extinct only when no living members remain anywhere. Losing a species from one forest is not the same thing.
scenes.visual: Transform the forest without cutting away. One tree fades GREY while the others stay GREEN. A living green tree drops YELLOW seeds and seedlings rise beside it. A small bird flies to a neighboring forest and lands there, still alive, while the rooted trees stay. Then zoom out: every chestnut in the first forest fades GREY while chestnuts in a distant forest stay GREEN. Label the comparison 'local loss is not extinction'.
scenes.narration: After a change, some members of a population die and some live. Living members may reproduce. Some migrate, meaning they move elsewhere, where they must still survive. A species is extinct only when no living members remain anywhere. Losing a species from one forest is not the same thing.

scenes.tts: Now look inside each tree. The blue bar represents inherited resistance, the ability to hold off the blight. Different bar heights show genetic variation in this useful trait. The tree cannot raise its bar because danger arrives. It begins with traits inherited from its parents.
scenes.caption: Now look inside each tree. The blue bar represents inherited resistance, the ability to hold off the blight. Different bar heights show genetic variation in this useful trait. The tree cannot raise its bar because danger arrives. It begins with traits inherited from its parents.
scenes.visual: Return to the original forest and zoom into four trunks. Show one vertical BLUE bar inside each, with different starting heights. Add the brief label 'inherited resistance'. A red wave approaches. One short bar tries to rise, then springs back to its starting height as a crossed-out thought bubble 'need does not change traits' appears. Thin lines connect each tree to two parent silhouettes behind it.
scenes.narration: Now look inside each tree. The blue bar represents inherited resistance, the ability to hold off the blight. Different bar heights show genetic variation in this useful trait. The tree cannot raise its bar because danger arrives. It begins with traits inherited from its parents.

scenes.tts: Red cankers spread through the bark. Trees with shorter blue bars are more likely to fade. A taller bar does not promise survival. It only changes the chance. Survivors that make yellow seeds can pass inherited traits into the next generation.
scenes.caption: Red cankers spread through the bark. Trees with shorter blue bars are more likely to fade. A taller bar does not promise survival. It only changes the chance. Survivors that make yellow seeds can pass inherited traits into the next generation.
scenes.visual: RED canker bands widen around trunks while all BLUE bars remain visible. Two short-bar trees fade GREY; one short-bar tree stays green to show chance. A tall-bar tree also wavers before remaining green, so the picture never promises survival. Yellow seeds fall only from two surviving trees. Seedlings rise with blue bars near their parents' heights. Mark the whole sequence 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Red cankers spread through the bark. Trees with shorter blue bars are more likely to fade. A taller bar does not promise survival. It only changes the chance. Survivors that make yellow seeds can pass inherited traits into the next generation.

scenes.tts: Compare these forests. Every tree in the narrow forest has a short resistance bar. The varied forest includes short, middle, and taller bars. Which forest is more likely to leave seed-making survivors after the blight?
scenes.caption: Compare these forests. Every tree in the narrow forest has a short resistance bar. The varied forest includes short, middle, and taller bars. Which forest is more likely to leave seed-making survivors after the blight?
scenes.visual: Split the carried forest into two equal panels. LEFT: six green trees with equally short BLUE bars. RIGHT: six green trees with BLUE bars ranging from short to tall. A RED blight front waits at the bottom of both panels. Put the question across the top. Leaves move gently and the red fronts shimmer.
scenes.narration: Compare these forests. Every tree in the narrow forest has a short resistance bar. The varied forest includes short, middle, and taller bars. Which forest is more likely to leave seed-making survivors after the blight?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the question on screen. The two red fronts pulse faintly, leaves sway, and blue bars glow. Do not show any outcome yet.

scenes.tts: The varied forest has a better chance because some helpful differences were already present. Yet it could still lose every tree. Variation in leaf shape or height would not solve this problem. The difference must help with this change. Helpful differences can appear later or arrive from elsewhere, but a fast change may leave too little time.
scenes.caption: The varied forest has a better chance because some helpful differences were already present. Yet it could still lose every tree. Variation in leaf shape or height would not solve this problem. The difference must help with this change. Helpful differences can appear later or arrive from elsewhere, but a fast change may leave too little time.
scenes.visual: Send the RED front through both panels. All left trees fade GREY in this schematic run. On the right, several fade but two with taller BLUE bars stay green and drop YELLOW seeds. Mark it 'schematic'. Briefly swap the blue bars for varied leaf shapes; all leaves receive the same red canker, then restore the resistance bars. A small clock spins quickly as a faint new blue bar approaches too late from beyond the frame.
scenes.narration: The varied forest has a better chance because some helpful differences were already present. Yet it could still lose every tree. Variation in leaf shape or height would not solve this problem. The difference must help with this change. Helpful differences can appear later or arrive from elsewhere, but a fast change may leave too little time.

scenes.tts: Green trees remain after the blight. If they never make seeds, their population still has no next generation. Now yellow seeds fall and seedlings rise. Here is the rule. When environments change, populations survive only if some members survive and reproduce.
scenes.caption: Green trees remain after the blight. If they never make seeds, their population still has no next generation. Now yellow seeds fall and seedlings rise. Here is the rule. When environments change, populations survive only if some members survive and reproduce.
scenes.visual: Clear to two surviving GREEN trees in the same forest. First show empty ground and a generation arrow that stops at the trees. Then pollen drifts between the two trees, YELLOW seeds appear, fall, and transform into seedlings as the arrow continues. Build the rule in white text above the growing seedlings, one clause at a time. Keep the trees and seedlings moving gently.
scenes.narration: Green trees remain after the blight. If they never make seeds, their population still has no next generation. Now yellow seeds fall and seedlings rise. Here is the rule. When environments change, populations survive only if some members survive and reproduce.

scenes.tts: A bird can leave a changed place. A rooted chestnut cannot, though seeds may spread its kind over time. Habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and invasive species create different challenges. The same test remains: can any members survive and reproduce?
scenes.caption: A bird can leave a changed place. A rooted chestnut cannot, though seeds may spread its kind over time. Habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and invasive species create different challenges. The same test remains: can any members survive and reproduce?
scenes.visual: Keep the forest centered. A bird crosses the frame while the green trunks remain anchored by visible roots. Yellow seeds drift only a short distance. Around the forest edge, transform one RED blight cloud into four labeled schematic pressures in sequence: 'habitat loss', 'pollution', 'climate change', and 'invasive species'. At most one label is prominent at a time. The seedling generation arrow stays visible.
scenes.narration: A bird can leave a changed place. A rooted chestnut cannot, though seeds may spread its kind over time. Habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and invasive species create different challenges. The same test remains: can any members survive and reproduce?

scenes.tts: Follow the forest once more. Red blight arrives. Blue resistance differs. Some trees remain, and yellow seeds start another generation. A population continues only when living members make a next generation.
scenes.caption: Follow the forest once more. Red blight arrives. Blue resistance differs. Some trees remain, and yellow seeds start another generation. A population continues only when living members make a next generation.
scenes.visual: Replay the carried world as one smooth transformation: red specks enter, blue bars stay fixed, several trees fade grey, and surviving green trees drop yellow seeds. Seedlings rise and replace the faded silhouettes. A single bright generation arrow sweeps from parents to seedlings.
scenes.narration: Follow the forest once more. Red blight arrives. Blue resistance differs. Some trees remain, and yellow seeds start another generation. A population continues only when living members make a next generation.

scenes.tts: This rule names a requirement, not a guarantee. A model forest is not a real forest. Next, test the rule in a model forest. Then read the real American chestnut data below.

scenes.visual: Mark the animated forest 'model'. Slide it left while a blank evidence table frame grows on the right, labeled 'real data'. Do not add values or answer any lesson data question. A white arrow points down toward the lesson text.

scenes.visual: Dim the forest but keep leaves and seedlings moving slowly. Show one centered line only in large white text: 'When environments change, populations survive only if some members survive and reproduce.'
